young.html: Rousseau's most famous book begins with a startling sentence: "Man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains." He meant that people are born with freedom, but live under rulers and laws they didn't choose.

Rousseau asked: how could people live together under laws and still be free? His answer was a kind of promise, a social contract. Everyone joins together and agrees to obey laws that the whole people makes for the good of all. When you obey a law that you helped make, you are obeying yourself.
Rousseau called the people's shared wish for the common good the general will. It isn't just what most people want at the moment. It is what is good for everyone together.

young.name: gb-sovereign-share
young.cap: Change the number of citizens and see each person's share of the vote.

young.html: A class law. As a family, decide on one rule that everyone will keep for a week (for example, "Phones stay out of the kitchen at dinner"). Everyone gets a vote, and the rule applies to everyone, grown-ups too. At the end of the week, talk: did it feel different to follow a rule you helped make?

full.html: The Social Contract (1762) appeared the same year as Rousseau's novel on education, Emile. Both were condemned and burned in Paris and in his native Geneva, and Rousseau fled. The book's question is not how governments began, but what could make them legitimate:

full.text: Man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains. One thinks himself the master of others, and still remains a greater slave than they. How did this change come about? I do not know. What can make it legitimate? That question I think I can answer.
full.work: The Social Contract, Book I, ch. 1
full.author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
full.ed: The Social Contract & Discourses, Everyman's Library, J. M. Dent, London, and E. P. Dutton, New York

full.html: Force can't make right, Rousseau argues: if might made right, the right would vanish the moment the might did. Nor can a people give itself away to a master, since giving up one's freedom is giving up being human.

full.text: The contract and the general will

full.html: The solution is a contract in which each person gives himself and all his rights to the whole community, so that the conditions are the same for all and no one has an interest in making them burdensome. In return each becomes an equal member of the sovereign, the people as law-maker. Rousseau distinguishes the general will, which aims at the common interest, from the will of all, which is only the sum of private wishes. The general will can't be represented: laws must be approved by the people themselves.

Key terms. Sovereign: the whole people making law. Government: the officials who carry out the law, a go-between, never the sovereign itself. General will: the will for the common good. Law: an act of the general will about matters common to all.

Rousseau's most troubling line says that whoever refuses to obey the general will "shall be compelled to do so by the whole body," which, he says, "means nothing less than that he will be forced to be free" (Book I, ch. 7). Readers have argued over it ever since.
In Book III Rousseau turns to government. He uses a bit of arithmetic to show why large states are harder to keep free:

full.text: Suppose the State is composed of ten thousand citizens. The Sovereign can only be considered collectively and as a body; but each member, as being a subject, is regarded as an individual: thus the Sovereign is to the subject as ten thousand to one, i. e. each member of the State has as his share only a ten-thousandth part of the sovereign authority, although he is wholly under its control.
full.work: The Social Contract, Book III, ch. 1
full.author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
full.ed: The Social Contract & Discourses, Everyman's Library, J. M. Dent, London, and E. P. Dutton, New York

full.name: gb-sovereign-share
full.cap: Rousseau's ratio: each citizen's share of sovereignty is 1 / N. The larger the state, the smaller the share, though each is still wholly under the law.

full.html: Democracy, aristocracy and monarchy each suit different sizes of state; Rousseau thinks true democracy fits only a small people of great virtue, and that elective aristocracy is often the best government. The book ends with a chapter on civil religion: a short public creed (a God, a life to come, the sanctity of the social contract and the laws) together with tolerance of all religions that tolerate others. Critics have found this chapter one of the hardest to square with freedom of conscience.
Confusing the general will with majority vote. A vote is Rousseau's way of finding the general will, and he says it works only when citizens vote for the common good and are not split into factions.

deep.html: Leaders of the French Revolution, especially the Jacobins, honored Rousseau and moved his remains to the Panthéon in 1794. Kant admired him so much that, it was said, he once skipped his daily walk to keep reading Emile. Supporters see in the Social Contract a powerful case for popular sovereignty, equality before the law and citizenship as active self-government.

Critics, among them Benjamin Constant in the 19th century and several 20th-century historians, argued that the general will and "forced to be free" could be used to justify states that override individual rights in the name of the people. Defenders answer that Rousseau insists on laws applying equally to all and on the sovereign's limits. Comparing Rousseau with Locke and Montesquieu, who stress representation and divided powers, is one of the great debates of this era.
